name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVINGCHARGESANDMAGNETISM_ASSERTIONREASON_Q01 - Circular motion of charge in uniform magnetic field

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field executes uniform circular motion with a constant speed.

Reason (R): The magnetic force \(q(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\) acts perpendicular to the velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) of the charged particle, so it performs zero work and cannot change the speed of the particle.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When a charge \(q\) moves with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) in a uniform magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\), the magnetic force is given by the Lorentz magnetic force formula \(\mathbf{F} = q(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\). By the definition of the vector cross product, \(\mathbf{F}\) is always perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{v}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
When \(\mathbf{v}\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{B}\), the magnitude of the magnetic force is \(F = qvB\sin 90^\circ = qvB\), which is constant and directed perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity. A force of constant magnitude always perpendicular to velocity acts as a centripetal force, producing uniform circular motion of radius \(r = \frac{mv}{qB}\) at constant speed. Therefore, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
The work done by a force over an infinitesimal displacement \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{v}\,\mathrm{d}t\) is \(\mathrm{d}W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{v})\,\mathrm{d}t\). Since \(\mathbf{F} \perp \mathbf{v}\), \(\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\), so the work done is zero. By the work-energy theorem, the kinetic energy \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\) and hence the speed \(v\) remain constant. Therefore, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Relationship and Final Conclusion
Because the magnetic force does zero work and only changes the direction of velocity while keeping its magnitude constant, it provides the centripetal force needed for uniform circular motion. Thus, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVINGCHARGESANDMAGNETISM_ASSERTIONREASON_Q02 - Force between two parallel current carrying conductors

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Two long, straight, parallel conductors carrying steady currents in the same direction attract each other.

Reason (R): Parallel currents repel each other in the same way that like-signed static electric charges repel each other.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A current-carrying conductor sets up a magnetic field around itself given by \(B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}\) at distance \(d\), and a second parallel conductor carrying current in this field experiences a magnetic force \(\mathbf{F} = I(\mathbf{l} \times \mathbf{B})\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Consider two parallel conductors carrying currents \(I_a\) and \(I_b\) in the same direction. By the right-hand thumb rule, the magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}_a\) produced by the first conductor at the location of the second conductor is perpendicular to it. Applying the cross product \(I_b(\mathbf{L} \times \mathbf{B}_a)\), the force on the second conductor is directed towards the first conductor. Similarly, the first conductor experiences an equal force towards the second conductor. Hence, parallel currents attract each other, so the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
In electrostatics, like charges repel each other. However, in magnetostatics, parallel (like-directed) currents attract each other, whereas antiparallel (oppositely directed) currents repel each other. Therefore, the Reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The Assertion is correct, but the Reason is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVINGCHARGESANDMAGNETISM_ASSERTIONREASON_Q03 - Magnetic force on stationary charge and tesla unit

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): A stationary electric charge placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences zero magnetic force.

Reason (R): The SI unit of magnetic field is the tesla (\(\text{T}\)), which is equivalent to \(1\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}/(\text{C}\cdot\text{m})\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The magnetic force acting on a point charge \(q\) moving with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) in a magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) is \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{magnetic}} = q(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\), with magnitude \(F = qvB\sin\theta\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
For a stationary charge, the speed is \(|\mathbf{v}| = 0\). Substituting \(v = 0\) into the magnetic force equation gives \(F = q(0)B\sin\theta = 0\). Only a moving charge experiences a magnetic force. Thus, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
From the relation \(F = qvB\sin\theta\), the dimensions and SI unit of \(B\) are obtained as \([B] = [F / (qv)]\), giving units of \(\frac{\text{N}}{\text{C} \cdot (\text{m/s})} = \text{N}\cdot\text{s}/(\text{C}\cdot\text{m})\), which is named the tesla (\(\text{T}\)). Thus, the Reason is also correct.

Step 4: Relationship and Final Conclusion
Although both statements are true, the definition of the SI unit of magnetic field (tesla) does not explain why a stationary charge experiences zero magnetic force (which is due to the velocity dependence \(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}\)). Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVINGCHARGESANDMAGNETISM_ASSERTIONREASON_Q04 - Biot-Savart law angle dependence along element

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): According to the Biot-Savart law, the magnetic field due to an infinitesimal current element \(I\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{l}\) at any point lying along the line of the current element is maximum.

Reason (R): The magnitude of the magnetic field due to a current element \(I\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{l}\) at a distance \(r\) is given by \(|\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}| = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,\mathrm{d}l\sin\theta}{r^2}\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{l}\) and the displacement vector \(\mathbf{r}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Biot-Savart law expresses the magnetic field \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}\) produced by an infinitesimal current element \(I\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{l}\) at a point located at displacement \(\mathbf{r}\) as \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} \times \mathbf{r}}{r^3}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
Using the property of the cross product \(|\mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} \times \mathbf{r}| = \mathrm{d}l\,r\sin\theta\), the magnitude of \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}\) simplifies to \(|\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}| = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,\mathrm{d}l\sin\theta}{r^2}\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{l}\) and \(\mathbf{r}\). Therefore, the Reason is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Assertion
For any point lying along the line of the current element, \(\mathbf{r}\) is either parallel (\(\theta = 0^\circ\)) or antiparallel (\(\theta = 180^\circ\)) to \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{l}\). In both cases, \(\sin\theta = 0\), which gives \(|\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}| = 0\) (minimum, not maximum). The field is maximum at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) for a given \(r\). Therefore, the Assertion is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The Assertion is incorrect, but the Reason is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVINGCHARGESANDMAGNETISM_ASSERTIONREASON_Q05 - Cyclotron frequency independence of speed and radius

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The frequency of revolution (cyclotron frequency) of a charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field is independent of its speed and the radius of its circular orbit.

Reason (R): The radius of the circular path is directly proportional to the speed of the particle (\(r = \frac{mv}{qB}\)), so the speed cancels out in the expression for the time period \(T = \frac{2\pi r}{v}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A particle of mass \(m\) and charge \(q\) moves with speed \(v\) perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of magnitude \(B\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The motion is non-relativistic, so \(m\) is constant, and the magnetic force \(qvB\) provides the entire centripetal force \(\frac{mv^2}{r}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Equating centripetal force to magnetic force: \(\frac{mv^2}{r} = qvB\). The time period of one revolution is \(T = \frac{2\pi r}{v}\), and the frequency is \(\nu = \frac{1}{T}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Solving for the radius gives \(r = \frac{mv}{qB}\), which is directly proportional to \(v\). Substituting \(r\) into the time period gives \(T = \frac{2\pi}{v}\left(\frac{mv}{qB}\right) = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}\). Consequently, the cyclotron frequency is \(\nu = \frac{qB}{2\pi m}\), which depends only on \(q\), \(B\), and \(m\), and is independent of \(v\) and \(r\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both the Assertion and the Reason are mathematically and physically consistent, and the cancellation of \(v\) in \(T = \frac{2\pi r}{v}\) directly explains why the cyclotron frequency is independent of speed and radius. Thus, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVINGCHARGESANDMAGNETISM_ASSERTIONREASON_Q06 - Conversion of moving coil galvanometer into voltmeter

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): To convert a moving coil galvanometer into a voltmeter, a large resistance is connected in series with the galvanometer coil.

Reason (R): Connecting a large resistance in series decreases the total resistance of the voltmeter so that it draws a large current from the circuit.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A voltmeter is connected in parallel across a section of a circuit to measure the potential difference without appreciably altering the current flowing through that section.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
To prevent the voltmeter from drawing significant current from the main circuit, its total resistance must be very large. Connecting a large resistance \(R\) in series with the galvanometer of resistance \(R_G\) yields a total resistance \(R_G + R \simeq R\), which is large. Therefore, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Connecting a resistor \(R\) in series *increases* the total resistance to \(R_G + R\) (rather than decreasing it), which ensures that the voltmeter draws a very *small* current (rather than a large current) from the circuit. Therefore, the Reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The Assertion is correct, but the Reason is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVINGCHARGESANDMAGNETISM_ASSERTIONREASON_Q07 - Magnetic field inside straight wire and closed loops

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Inside a long straight wire of circular cross-section (radius \(a\)) carrying a uniformly distributed steady current \(I\), the magnitude of the magnetic field at a distance \(r < a\) from the axis is directly proportional to \(r\).

Reason (R): Magnetic field lines always form closed loops, unlike electrostatic field lines which originate from positive charges and terminate at negative charges.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the Assertion
Consider a circular Amperian loop of radius \(r < a\) concentric with the wire's axis. Since the current \(I\) is uniformly distributed over the cross-sectional area \(\pi a^2\), the current enclosed by the loop of area \(\pi r^2\) is \(I_e = I\left(\frac{\pi r^2}{\pi a^2}\right) = \frac{Ir^2}{a^2}\). By Ampere's circuital law, \(B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_e = \mu_0 \frac{Ir^2}{a^2}\), which gives \(B = \left(\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a^2}\right)r\). Thus, \(B \propto r\) for \(r < a\), so the Assertion is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reason
Magnetic monopoles do not exist, and magnetic field lines around currents always form continuous closed loops, whereas electrostatic field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges (or at infinity). Therefore, the Reason is also correct.

Step 3: Relationship and Final Conclusion
While both statements are true, the fact that magnetic field lines form closed loops does not explain why \(B \propto r\) inside a uniform current-carrying wire (which arises from the uniform current density and enclosed current \(I_e \propto r^2\)). Hence, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVINGCHARGESANDMAGNETISM_ASSERTIONREASON_Q08 - Stable equilibrium of current loop in magnetic field

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): A planar current-carrying loop placed in a uniform external magnetic field is in stable equilibrium when its magnetic dipole moment \(\mathbf{m}\) is parallel to the magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\).

Reason (R): When \(\mathbf{m}\) is parallel to \(\mathbf{B}\), the torque \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{m} \times \mathbf{B}\) is zero, and any small angular rotation of the loop produces a restoring torque that brings it back to its original orientation.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A planar current loop with magnetic moment \(\mathbf{m} = I\mathbf{A}\) in a uniform magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) experiences a torque \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{m} \times \mathbf{B}\) of magnitude \(\tau = mB\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\mathbf{m}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion and Reason
When \(\mathbf{m}\) is parallel to \(\mathbf{B}\), \(\theta = 0^\circ\), so \(\tau = mB\sin 0^\circ = 0\), establishing rotational equilibrium. If the loop is slightly displaced by a small angle \(\Delta\theta\), the torque \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{m} \times \mathbf{B}\) acts in a direction that opposes the displacement and rotates \(\mathbf{m}\) back toward \(\mathbf{B}\). By definition, an equilibrium state where small perturbations generate a restoring torque is a stable equilibrium. (In contrast, when \(\mathbf{m}\) is antiparallel to \(\mathbf{B}\), \(\theta = 180^\circ\), any small rotation produces a torque that increases the deviation, making it unstable equilibrium.)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason correctly explains why the parallel orientation corresponds to stable equilibrium.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVINGCHARGESANDMAGNETISM_ASSERTIONREASON_Q09 - Current sensitivity versus voltage sensitivity in galvanometer

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Increasing the current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer by doubling the number of turns \(N\) in the coil automatically doubles its voltage sensitivity.

Reason (R): When the number of turns \(N\) is doubled, the current sensitivity \(\frac{\phi}{I} = \frac{NAB}{k}\) doubles, but the coil resistance \(R\) also doubles due to the doubled wire length, leaving the voltage sensitivity \(\frac{\phi}{V} = \frac{NAB}{kR}\) unchanged.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A moving coil galvanometer has \(N\) turns, coil area \(A\), radial magnetic field \(B\), spring torsional constant \(k\), and coil resistance \(R\). The number of turns is changed from \(N\) to \(N' = 2N\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Each turn has the same perimeter and wire cross-section, so the total length of the wire (and hence the resistance \(R\) of the galvanometer coil) is directly proportional to \(N\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Current sensitivity is \(\frac{\phi}{I} = \frac{NAB}{k}\), and voltage sensitivity is \(\frac{\phi}{V} = \left(\frac{NAB}{k}\right)\frac{1}{R}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
When \(N \rightarrow 2N\), the current sensitivity becomes \(\left(\frac{\phi}{I}\right)' = \frac{(2N)AB}{k} = 2\left(\frac{\phi}{I}\right)\), so it doubles. However, since the wire length doubles, the resistance becomes \(R' = 2R\). Substituting into the voltage sensitivity expression gives \(\left(\frac{\phi}{V}\right)' = \frac{(2N)AB}{k(2R)} = \frac{NAB}{kR} = \frac{\phi}{V}\), which remains unchanged.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, doubling the number of turns does not increase voltage sensitivity. The Assertion is incorrect, and the Reason is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVINGCHARGESANDMAGNETISM_ASSERTIONREASON_Q10 - Flexible irregular current loop assumes circular shape

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): A flexible wire loop of irregular shape carrying a steady current and placed in a uniform external magnetic field changes to a circular shape with its plane perpendicular to the magnetic field.

Reason (R): For a given perimeter, a circle encloses the maximum area, so this circular shape oriented normal to the magnetic field maximizes the magnetic flux through the loop.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A flexible current-carrying loop in an external magnetic field experiences magnetic forces \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{F} = I\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} \times \mathbf{B}\) on its elements, which tend to orient and stretch the loop into a configuration of minimum potential energy and maximum magnetic flux.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion and Reason
The magnetic flux through a planar loop of area \(\mathbf{A}\) in a uniform field \(\mathbf{B}\) is \(\Phi_B = \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{A} = BA\cos\theta\). To maximize this flux, two conditions must be met: first, \(\cos\theta = 1\) (\(\theta = 0^\circ\)), meaning the area vector \(\mathbf{A}\) is parallel to \(\mathbf{B}\) (plane of the loop perpendicular to \(\mathbf{B}\)); second, the enclosed area \(A\) must be as large as possible for the fixed perimeter of the wire. By the isoperimetric property, a circle encloses the maximum possible area for a given perimeter. Therefore, the magnetic forces pull the flexible wire outward into a circular shape normal to \(\mathbf{B}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVINGCHARGESANDMAGNETISM_ASSERTIONREASON_Q11 - Magnetic field inside and outside a solenoid

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Inside an ideal very long solenoid carrying a steady current \(I\) with \(n\) turns per unit length, the magnetic field is uniform, directed along the axis, and given by \(B = \mu_0 n I\).

Reason (R): Applying Ampere's circuital law to a rectangular loop enclosing \(nh\) turns gives \(Bh = \mu_0 n I h\) because the magnetic field outside even a finite solenoid is strictly zero at all exterior points.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a solenoid with \(n\) turns per unit length carrying current \(I\), Ampere's circuital law \(\oint \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} = \mu_0 I_e\) applied to a rectangular Amperian loop \(abcd\) (with side \(ab\) of length \(h\) inside and parallel to the axis, \(cd\) outside, and transverse sides \(bc\) and \(ad\) perpendicular to the axis) is used to find the interior field.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In the ideal limit of a very long solenoid (length much greater than radius), the exterior magnetic field approaches zero and the interior field becomes uniform and everywhere parallel to the axis. Since the transverse segments contribute zero and the exterior segment contributes zero, \(Bh = \mu_0 (nh)I\), yielding \(B = \mu_0 n I\). Therefore, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
For a *finite* solenoid, the magnetic field at exterior points (such as the exterior mid-point) is weak and directed opposite to the interior field, not strictly zero at all points. The exterior field only approaches zero in the idealised limit of an infinitely long solenoid. Therefore, the claim in the Reason that the field outside a finite solenoid is strictly zero at all exterior points is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The Assertion is correct, but the Reason is incorrect.
